chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala from Aban from Zurara from one of the Imams (peace be upon them both) that he said:
"Indeed, eating the crow is not forbidden; rather, the forbidden is what God has forbidden in His Book, but the souls shy away from much of it out of aversion."

Because His Excellency's statement in the first narration, 'and its flesh is not eaten,' we interpret as disliked (karahah) and not as strictly prohibited (hazr), based on the explicit statement in the second narration from His Excellency, 'Indeed, eating it is not forbidden,' and that one shies away from such things out of aversion. There is no contradiction between them on this basis, and this interpretation does not contradict what was narrated:
ai.seo_question: Is eating crow meat forbidden or just disliked in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from the Tahdhib al-Ahkam illustrates the Shia juristic principle of distinguishing between divine prohibition (haram) and natural aversion (tazaqqun), resolving apparent contradictions in prophetic traditions by interpreting 'not eaten' as a recommendation rather than a strict ban. It highlights the scholarly method of harmonizing texts by attributing dietary restrictions to human disposition rather than explicit Quranic decree, a key concept in Usul al-Fiqh.
